helicoprion:eswiki:6.title: Helicoprion (Naturaleza de la espiral de los dientes)

facts.statement: The animal is classified under the genus Helicoprion.
facts.quote: taxon: Helicoprion

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Helicoprion bessonowi.
facts.quote: type_species: Helicoprion bessonowi

facts.statement: Two recognized species are H. davisii, described by Woodward in 1886, and H. ergassaminon, described by Bendix-Almgreen in 1966.
facts.quote: subdivision: *H. davisii (Woodward, 1886) H. ergassaminon Bendix-Almgreen, 1966

facts.statement: The genus was described by Karpinsky in 1899.
facts.quote: authority: Karpinsky, 1899

facts.statement: Fossils of Helicoprion range from the Cisuralian to the Guadalupian stages, specifically from the Artinskian to the Roadian.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cisuralian to Guadalupian (Artinskian to Roadian)

facts.statement: Helicoprion lived during the Early to Middle Permian, approximately 290 to 270 million years ago.
facts.quote: lived from the Early to the Middle Permian, about 290-270 million years ago

facts.statement: Helicoprion belongs to the extinct order Eugeneodontiformes, which is part of the clade Holocephali.
facts.quote: Helicoprion is a member of the Eugeneodontiformes, an extinct order of cartilaginous fish within the clade Holocephali

facts.statement: Helicoprion is the type genus of the family Helicoprionidae, characterized by distinctive tooth whorls.
facts.quote: It is also the type genus of the Helicoprionidae, a family of eugeneodonts characterised by distinctive tooth structures called tooth whorls

facts.statement: Helicoprion was first named in 1899 by Alexander Karpinsky based on fossils found in Russia and Australia.
facts.quote: Helicoprion was first named in 1899 by Alexander Karpinsky on the basis of fossils discovered in Russia and Australia

facts.statement: The generic name Helicoprion means "spiral saw".
facts.quote: the generic name meaning "spiral saw"

facts.statement: Following a 2013 revision, only three species are recognized: H. bessonowi, H. davisii, and H. ergassaminon.
facts.quote: only H. bessonowi, H. davisii, and H. ergassaminon are recognized following a 2013 revision

facts.statement: Studies suggest the tooth whorls were located in the lower jaw and specialized for grasping and slicing soft-bodied prey like cephalopods.
facts.quote: studies based on specimens preserving jaw cartilage indicate that they were positioned in the lower jaw and were specialised for grasping and slicing soft-bodied prey such as cephalopods

facts.statement: Helicoprion was pelagic and had a cosmopolitan distribution, as fossils are found in marine deposits worldwide.
facts.quote: Fossils of Helicoprion are known from marine deposits worldwide, indicating that it was pelagic and had a cosmopolitan distribution

facts.statement: The first specimen was discovered in Western Australia in a tributary of the Gascoyne River by a gold prospector named Mr. Davis.
facts.quote: It was discovered in Western Australia in a tributary of the Gascoyne River by a gold prospector named Mr. Davis

facts.statement: The first specimen is now housed in the Western Australian Museum under catalogue number WAMAG 9080.
facts.quote: Now housed in the Western Australian Museum under the catalogue WAMAG 9080

facts.statement: The fossil was not found in situ, so its precise stratigraphic origin remains uncertain.
facts.quote: the fossil was not found in situ, thus its precise stratigraphic origin remains uncertain

facts.statement: In 1886, Woodward described the specimen as a new species of Edestus, naming it Edestus davisii.
facts.quote: In a 1886 publication, Woodward finally described the specimen as representing a new species of Edestus, which he named Edestus davisii

facts.statement: Karpinsky assigned the fossils to a new genus named Helicoprion, with H. bessonowi as the type species.
facts.quote: Karpinsky assigned them to a new genus, which he named Helicoprion, with H. bessonowi as the type species

facts.statement: The most complete specimen, catalogued as TsNIGR 1/1865, was designated the lectotype by Dmitry Obruchev in a 1964 publication.
facts.quote: Among the six specimens described by Karpinsky, the most complete of them, later catalogued as TsNIGR 1/1865 in the collections of the Central Research Geological Museum in Saint Petersburg, was designated as the lectotype by Russian paleontologist Dmitry Obruchev in a 1964 publication

facts.statement: The lectotype specimen was stolen in 1998 and later recovered by David J. Ward with the help of an anonymous fossil dealer.
facts.quote: This same specimen was stolen in 1998 and was eventually recovered by British paleontologist David J. Ward with the assistance of an anonymous fossil dealer

facts.statement: Eastman challenged Karpinsky's interpretation in 1902 by assigning the species to the genus Campyloprion.
facts.quote: However, this interpretation was challenged as early as 1902 by American paleontologist Charles R. Eastman, who assigned the species to Campyloprion, a newly erected and closely related taxon

facts.statement: Oliver Perry Hay transferred the species to the genus Toxoprion in 1909.
facts.quote: In 1909, his colleague Oliver Perry Hay transferred the species once again, this time to Toxoprion, another newly established, related genus

facts.statement: H. ergassaminon was first described in 1966 by Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen based on fossils in Idaho universities.
facts.quote: H. ergassaminon was first described in 1966 by Danish ichthyologist Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen in a monograph devoted to several Helicoprion fossils housed in the paleontological collections of various universities in Idaho, USA

facts.statement: The holotype, nicknamed "Idaho 5", was discovered in an abandoned mine near Fort Hall.
facts.quote: This latter, nicknamed "Idaho 5" and discovered in a now-abandoned mine near Fort Hall

facts.statement: The holotype was rediscovered in 2017 at the Natural History Museum of Denmark and transferred to Idaho State University in 2023.
facts.quote: The holotype was finally rediscovered in 2017 during the recataloguing of the fossil collections at the Natural History Museum of Denmark, before being transferred in 2023 to the Idaho State University in Pocatello

facts.statement: Hay described the species Lissoprion ferrieri in 1907 and 1909 from fossils found in phosphate deposits along the Idaho–Wyoming border.
facts.quote: In his 1907 and 1909 works, Hay erected a new genus and species of eugeneodont, Lissoprion ferrieri, which he described from three fossil specimens originating from phosphate deposits along the Idaho–Wyoming border.

facts.statement: Karpinsky reclassified the taxon as Helicoprion ferrieri in 1911.
facts.quote: Karpinsky to reclassify the taxon as H. ferrieri in 1911

facts.statement: Harry E. Wheeler named the species Helicoprion sierrensis and Helicoprion nevadensis in 1939 from fossils found in California and Nevada.
facts.quote: In 1939, American geologist Harry E. Wheeler named two additional Helicoprion species, H. sierrensis and H. nevadensis, based on type specimens from California and Nevada, respectively.

facts.statement: Federico K. G. Müllerried described the species Helicoprion mexicanus in 1945 from a fossil found in Coahuila, Mexico.
facts.quote: In 1945, geologist Federico K. G. Müllerried described the species H. mexicanus on the basis of a poorly preserved partial tooth whorl bearing 10 teeth, discovered in the Mexican state of Coahuila.

facts.statement: Obruchev illustrated a fossil specimen of Helicoprion in 1953 from the Ural Mountains of Russia.
facts.quote: In 1953, Obruchev illustrated in his monograph a poorly preserved fossil specimen preserving the impression and root of two teeth, discovered in the Ural Mountains of Russia.

facts.statement: Stanisław Siedlecki named the species Helicoprion svalis in 1970 from fossils found in the Svalbard archipelago.
facts.quote: In 1970, Polish geologist Stanisław Siedlecki named the species H. svalis on the basis of isolated teeth and fragmentary tooth whorls recovered from the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard.

facts.statement: Xiao Hong Chen and colleagues described the species Helicoprion jingmenense in 2007 from a fossil found in Hubei Province, China.
facts.quote: In 2007, palaeontologist Xiao Hong Chen and colleagues described the species H. jingmenense from an almost complete tooth whorl discovered during road construction in Hubei Province, China.

facts.statement: Eastman proposed in 1903 that Campyloprion annectans belonged to the genus Helicoprion.
facts.quote: In 1903, shortly after establishing Campyloprion with C. annectans as its type species, Eastman apparently concluded that this taxon was sufficiently similar to Helicoprion to be reassigned as a distinct lineage within that genus.

facts.statement: Karpinsky described the species Helicoprion clerci in 1916 from fossils found near Krasnoufimsk.
facts.quote: In 1916, Karpinsky erected the species H. clerci on the basis of fragmentary remains of a large tooth whorl discovered near Krasnoufimsk

facts.statement: Dagmar Merino-Rodo and Philippe Janvier described the species Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi in 1986 from fossils near La Paz, Bolivia.
facts.quote: In 1986, the Bolivian geologist Dagmar Merino-Rodo and the French paleontologist Philippe Janvier described a second species, P. mariosuarezi, based on fossils unearthed near La Paz, Bolivia.

facts.statement: Karpinsky described the species Helicoprion ivanovi in 1922 from fossils found near Moscow.
facts.quote: In 1922, Karpinsky erected another species of Helicoprion, H. ivanovi, based on fossils discovered at a locality near Moscow.

facts.statement: Oleg Lebedev and colleagues reclassified Helicoprion ivanovi into the genus Karpinskiprion in 2022.
facts.quote: in 2022, Russian palaeontologist Oleg Lebedev and colleagues once again reclassified the species into its own genus, which they named Karpinskiprion.

facts.statement: Helicoprion had a skeleton made of cartilage.
facts.quote: Like other chondrichthyan fish, Helicoprion had a skeleton made of cartilage.

facts.statement: The cartilage around Helicoprion's jaws was mineralized, while the rest of the skeleton was likely unmineralized and decayed quickly.
facts.quote: Around the jaws, this cartilage was mineralized, but the rest of the skeleton was likely completely unmineralized and quickly disintegrated once it began to decay.

facts.statement: Helicoprion had a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body with triangular pectoral fins.
facts.quote: Eugeneodonts are characterized by a fusiform (streamlined, torpedo-shaped) body plan, with triangular pectoral fins.

facts.statement: Helicoprion had a single large triangular dorsal fin without a spine and a tall, forked caudal fin with two equally sized lobes.
facts.quote: They have a single large and triangular dorsal fin without a fin spine, and a tall, forked caudal fin, which externally appears to be homocercal (with two equally sized lobes).

facts.statement: Helicoprion lacked pelvic and anal fins.
facts.quote: Eugeneodonts also lack pelvic and anal fins

facts.statement: Tapanila suggested that the largest Helicoprion individuals could reach 9.7–12 meters in total length.
facts.quote: Tapanila has suggested a total length of 9.7-12 m for the largest Helicoprion individuals.

facts.statement: Tapanila and Pruitt regarded Helicoprion ferrieri as a junior synonym of Helicoprion davisii in their 2013 revision.
facts.quote: In their 2013 revision, Tapanila and Pruitt demonstrated that these traits vary naturally within a single Helicoprion species, so regarded H. ferrieri as a junior synonym of H. davisii.

facts.statement: Tapanila and Pruitt synonymized Helicoprion sierrensis with Helicoprion davisii and Helicoprion nevadensis with Helicoprion bessonowi in their 2013 revision.
facts.quote: In their 2013 revision, Tapanila and Pruitt demonstrated that the characters attributed to H. sierrensis fall within the natural range of variation seen in H. davisii, while those of H. nevadensis correspond to the growth stage of H. bessonowi.

facts.statement: Helicoprion mexicanus is regarded as a nomen dubium due to incomplete preservation.
facts.quote: Consequently, in the absence of more complete material attributable to the taxon, H. mexicanus is regarded as a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Tapanila and Pruitt classified the species described by Obruchev as a nomen nudum.
facts.quote: Tapanila and Pruitt classified this species as a nomen nudum.

facts.statement: Tapanila and Pruitt regarded Helicoprion svalis as a doubtful taxon in 2013 due to incomplete fossil material.
facts.quote: The authors of the 2013 revision considered H. svalis to be strongly similar to H. bessonowi, but could not formally synonymise the two due to the incompleteness of the fossil material, so regarded it as a doubtful taxon.

facts.statement: Tapanila and Pruitt regarded Helicoprion jingmenense as a junior synonym of Helicoprion davisii in their 2013 revision.
facts.quote: In their 2013 revision, though, Tapanila and Pruitt pointed out that the specimen is partially obscured by its surrounding matrix, which likely led to an underestimation of tooth height. Taking this into account, along with intraspecific variation, they regarded H. jingmenense as a junior synonym of H. davisii.

facts.statement: Naugolnykh and Naumkin proposed in 2018 and 2023 that Parahelicoprion may be a junior synonym of Helicoprion.
facts.quote: In 2018 and 2023, Russian palaeontologists Sergey V. Naugolnykh and Dmitry V. Naumkin proposed that Parahelicoprion may, in fact, represent a junior synonym of Helicoprion

facts.statement: Some authors continue to consider Parahelicoprion distinct from Helicoprion.
facts.quote: Other authors have continued to consider the genus to be distinct from Helicoprion.

facts.statement: Lebedev and colleagues reclassified Helicoprion ivanovi into the genus Karpinskiprion in 2022.
facts.quote: However, in 2022, Russian palaeontologist Oleg Lebedev and colleagues once again reclassified the species into its own genus, which they named Karpinskiprion.

facts.statement: Helicoprion was likely an active, open-water predatory fish.
facts.quote: This general body plan is shared by active, open-water predatory fish such as tuna, swordfish, and lamnid sharks.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Parahelicoprion is a distinct genus or a junior synonym of Helicoprion.
facts.quote: In 2018 and 2023, Russian palaeontologists Sergey V. Naugolnykh and Dmitry V. Naumkin proposed that Parahelicoprion may, in fact, represent a junior synonym of Helicoprion, suggesting that the genus may have been named on the basis of fossils belonging to exceptionally large and old individuals of the latter. Other authors have continued to consider the genus to be distinct from Helicoprion.

facts.statement: Most Helicoprion fossils consist of tooth whorls containing dozens of enameloid teeth arranged in a logarithmic spiral.
facts.quote: Almost all Helicoprion specimens are known solely from "tooth whorls", which consist of dozens of enameloid-covered teeth embedded within a single logarithmic spiral-shaped root.

facts.statement: The central juvenile teeth in the Helicoprion spiral are hooked, while other teeth are triangular, laterally compressed, and serrated.
facts.quote: The youngest and first teeth at the center of the spiral, referred to as the "juvenile tooth arch", are hooked, but all other teeth are generally triangular in shape, laterally compressed, and typically serrated.

facts.statement: Helicoprion teeth grow larger away from the spiral center, with the largest potentially exceeding 10 cm in height.
facts.quote: Tooth size increases away from the center of the spiral, with the largest teeth possibly exceeding 10 cm in height.

facts.statement: The three Helicoprion species are distinguished solely by differences in their tooth whorl anatomy.
facts.quote: The three species of Helicoprion differ only in the anatomy of their tooth whorls.

facts.statement: H. ergassaminon has an intermediate anatomy with tall, closely spaced crowns and tooth bases angled like H. davisii.
facts.quote: H. ergassaminon is roughly intermediate in anatomy between H. bessonowi and H. davisii, with tall but closely spaced crowns and tooth bases angled similarly to H. davisii.

facts.statement: CT scans of a specimen revealed a nearly complete set of articulated upper and lower jaws preserved in three dimensions.
facts.quote: CT scanning revealed a nearly complete set of upper and lower jaws, still in articulation and preserved in three dimensions.

facts.statement: The best-preserved Helicoprion specimen lacks a chondrocranium, the cartilage structure housing the brain and sensory organs.
facts.quote: The specimen does not preserve a chondrocranium, the cartilaginous structure that would have housed the brain and sensory organs.

facts.statement: Helicoprion possessed an autodiastylic jaw suspension where the palatoquadrate attached to the chondrocranium at two separate points without fusion.
facts.quote: Helicoprion had an autodiastylic jaw suspension, meaning that the inner edge of the palatoquadrate was firmly attached (but not fused) to the chondrocranium at two separate points.

facts.statement: The inner surface of the Helicoprion palatoquadrate was covered with small teeth approximately 2 mm wide.
facts.quote: The inner surface of the palatoquadrate was covered with numerous small (~2 mm wide) teeth.

facts.statement: Helicoprion's Meckel's cartilage features an additional projection before the joint with the palatoquadrate.
facts.quote: The Meckel's cartilage of Helicoprion has an additional projection right before the joint with the palatoquadrate.

facts.statement: Helicoprion scales are more strongly pointed than those of other eugeneodonts.
facts.quote: Compared to other eugeneodonts, the scales of Helicoprion are more strongly pointed.

facts.statement: Skull characteristics confirm Helicoprion belongs to the chondrichthyan subclass Holocephali or the broader group Euchondrocephali.
facts.quote: Skull data from IMNH 37899 reveal several characteristics, such as an autodiastylic (two-jointed) jaw suspension with a nonsuspensory hyomandibula, which confirm the placement of Helicoprion within the chondrichthyan subclass Holocephali (or the more broadly defined Euchondrocephali).

facts.statement: Helicoprion is classified as a member of the order Eugeneodontiformes, defined by midline tooth whorls and autodiastylic skulls.
facts.quote: Helicoprion can be characterized as a member of Eugeneodontiformes, an order of holocephalans that lived from the Devonian to Triassic periods and are defined by their tooth whorls along the midline of the jaw and autodiastylic skulls.

facts.statement: Helicoprion is placed within the Edestoidea subgroup of Eugeneodontiformes.
facts.quote: Within the Eugeneodontiformes, Helicoprion is placed within the Edestoidea, a group of eugeneodonts with particularly tall and angled symphyseal teeth.

facts.statement: Helicoprionidae members have large, arched tooth whorls supported by cartilage that add new teeth continuously at the spiral apex with forward-inclined bases.
facts.quote: Members of this family are distinguished by their large, strongly arched tooth whorls supported by cartilage, which do not replace teeth, but instead add new ones continuously at the apex of the spiral, with tooth bases inclined forward.

facts.statement: Helicoprion is unique in its family for having a closed spiral whorl that revolves multiple times, unlike the open spirals of other genera.
facts.quote: Helicoprion is unique among members of its family in possessing a closed (complete) spiral whorl, which revolves around itself multiple times, while the tooth whorls of other genera form an incomplete, open spiral.

facts.statement: Helicoprion lived during the Devonian to Triassic periods.
facts.quote: Eugeneodontiformes, an order of holocephalans that lived from the Devonian to Triassic periods and are defined by their tooth whorls along the midline of the jaw and autodiastylic skulls.

facts.statement: Relationships within the eugeneodont group remain unclear due to fragmentary fossil remains.
facts.quote: As most eugeneodonts are based on fragmentary tooth remains, relationships within the group remain unclear.

facts.statement: Helicoprion was likely a bite feeder rather than a suction feeder.
facts.quote: Helicoprion is thought to have been a bite feeder.

facts.statement: Biomechanical modeling suggests Helicoprion's teeth had distinct functions: front teeth snagged prey, middle teeth speared, and hind teeth punctured and pushed prey into the throat.
facts.quote: The foremost teeth served to snag and pull prey further into the mouth, while the middle teeth speared, and the hind teeth punctured and brought prey further into the throat.

facts.statement: Helicoprion likely captured prey with rapid jaw closures and then used repeated opening and closing motions to saw through it.
facts.quote: Helicoprion likely used a series of rapid, forceful jaw closures to initially capture and push prey deeper into the mouth, followed by repeated opening and closing of the jaw to saw through prey.

facts.statement: Estimates place Helicoprion's bite force between 1,192 and 2,391 Newtons with bite stresses between 397 and 797 million N/m².
facts.quote: At the three points of contact, the estimated bite force ranges between 1,192 and 2,391 N, with estimated bite stresses ranging from 397 to 797 e6N/m2 during prey contact.

facts.statement: The genus Helicoprion was established by Karpinsky in 1899.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Karpinsky, 1899

facts.statement: Helicoprion was an extinct cartilaginous fish of the order Eugeneodontiformes that first appeared in the Early Carboniferous (approx. 280 million years ago) and went extinct in the Late Triassic (approx. 225 million years ago).
facts.quote: Helicoprion (gr. "sierra en espiral") es un género extinto de peces cartilaginosos del orden Eugeneodontiformes, similar a los tiburones que surgió por primera vez en los océanos del Carbonífero inferior (hace unos 280 millones de años) y sobrevivió a la extinción masiva del Pérmico-Triásico, y terminó extinguiéndose en el Triásico Superior hace unos 225 millones de años.

facts.statement: The only known fossil remains of Helicoprion are teeth arranged in a spiral resembling a circular saw.
facts.quote: Los únicos restos fósiles conocidos eran los dientes, ordenados en una fantástica espiral que recuerda mucho una sierra circular.

facts.statement: Comparisons with other eugeneodontids suggest Helicoprion could have reached a length of about 7 meters.
facts.quote: Al compararlo con otros eugeneodóntidos, se piensa que el Helicoprion pudo haber alcanzado una talla de unos 7 metros de largo.

facts.statement: Helicoprion's sharp teeth imply that it was a carnivore.
facts.quote: Los dientes eran afilados, lo que implica que estos animales eran carnívoros.

facts.statement: Helicoprion fossils first appear in Late Carboniferous marine strata, proliferated during the Permian, and disappear from the record in the Early Triassic.
facts.quote: Los fósiles de las especies de Helicoprion aparecieron por primera vez en los estratos marinos del Carbonífero Superior, proliferando en gran medida durante el Pérmico, y desaparecen del registro durante el Triásico Inferior.

facts.statement: Helicoprion fossils have been found in the Ural Mountains, the Wandagee Mountains of Western Australia, China, and western North America including the Canadian Arctic and states such as New Mexico, Idaho, Nevada, Wyoming, Texas, Utah, and California.
facts.quote: Sus fósiles se han encontrado en los Montes Urales, en los Montes Wandagee de Australia Occidental, en China junto con los géneros relacionados Sinohelicoprion y Hunanohelicoprion, y en el oeste de América del Norte, incluyendo el Ártico canadiense, los estados de Nuevo México, Idaho, Nevada, Wyoming, Texas, Utah y California.

facts.statement: Hypotheses regarding the placement and identity of Helicoprion's tooth whorl were controversial from its initial discovery.
facts.quote: Hypotheses for the placement and identity of Helicoprion's tooth whorls were controversial since it was first discovered.

facts.statement: In 1900, Eastman supported the hypothesis that the tooth whorl was a defensive structure embedded in the animal's body rather than part of the mouth.
facts.quote: In 1900, the publication was reviewed by Eastman, who appreciated the paper as a whole, but derided the sketch of the supposed life position of the whorl. Though Eastman admitted that the teeth of the whorl were very similar to those of other chondrichthyans, he still supported the idea that the whorl may have been a defensive structure embedded into the body of the animal, rather than the mouth.

facts.statement: For a long time, the only known fossils of Helicoprion were its teeth, which were arranged in a spiral resembling a circular saw.
facts.quote: Hasta hace poco, los únicos fósiles conocidos de esta especie fueron los dientes, que se organizaban en una «espiral de dientes» que recuerda mucho a una sierra circular.

facts.statement: It was not until the discovery of the skull of a related shark genus, Ornithoprion, that it became clear the spiral set of teeth was located in the lower jaw.
facts.quote: No fue sino hasta el descubrimiento del cráneo de un género relacionado de tiburón Ornithoprion, cuando se hizo evidente que el conjunto de dientes en espiral se situaba en la mandíbula inferior.

facts.statement: The tooth-whorl contained all the teeth produced by an individual in the lower jaw, with new teeth pushing older ones toward the center of the spiral as the animal grew.
facts.quote: El diente-verticilo agrupaba todos los dientes producidos por un individuo en la mandíbula inferior, y a medida que el individuo crecía, se producían nuevos dientes que desplazaban hacia el centro de la espiral a los más viejos.

facts.statement: A 2008 reconstruction by Mary Parrish, Robert Purdy, Víctor Springer, and Matt Carrano places the tooth-whorl deepest in the throat, a conclusion not accepted by other studies.
facts.quote: Una reconstrucción de 2008, creado por Mary Parrish bajo la dirección de Robert Purdy, Víctor Springer y Matt Carrano para el Smithsonian, coloca el verticilo más profundo en la garganta, aunque otros estudios no han aceptado esta conclusión.

facts.statement: A 2013 study based on new data places the tooth-whorl at the back of the lower jaw, where it would occupy the entire mandibular arch.
facts.quote: Un estudio de 2013 sobre la base de nuevos datos coloca el diente-verticilo en la parte posterior de la mandíbula, en la que el diente-verticilo ocuparía todo el arco mandibular.

facts.statement: Although no complete Helicoprion skulls exist, related shark species having pointed snouts suggests Helicoprion may have possessed a similar feature.
facts.quote: Si bien no hay cráneos completos de Helicoprion, el hecho de que las especies relacionadas de tiburones tenían hocicos largos en punta sugiere que Helicoprion pudo también poseerlo así.

facts.statement: The genus Helicoprion was named by Karpinsky in 1899.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Helicoprion (genus), Karpinsky 1899

facts.statement: Helicoprion belongs to the parent group Helicoprionidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Helicoprionidae

facts.statement: Helicoprion is classified in the family Helicoprionidae.
facts.quote: Family: Helicoprionidae

facts.statement: Helicoprion is classified in the class Chondrichthyes.
facts.quote: Class: Chondrichthyes

facts.statement: Helicoprion lived from the Asselian to the Wuchiapingian stages, between 298.9 and 254.14 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Asselian to Wuchiapingian (298.9 to 254.14 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are 35 recorded fossil occurrences of Helicoprion.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 35
